module FixturesTestHelper
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  class_methods do
    def identify(label, column_type = :integer)
      if label.to_s.end_with?("_uuid")
        column_type = :uuid
        label = label.to_s.delete_suffix("_uuid")
      end

      # Rails passes :string for varchar columns, so handle both :uuid and :string
      return super(label, column_type) unless column_type.in?([ :uuid, :string ])
      generate_fixture_uuid(label)
    end

    private

    def generate_fixture_uuid(label)
      # Generate deterministic UUIDv7 for fixtures that sorts by fixture ID
      # This allows .first/.last to work as expected in tests
      # Use the same CRC32 algorithm as Rails' default fixture ID generation
      # so that UUIDs sort in the same order as integer IDs
      fixture_int = Zlib.crc32("fixtures/#{label}") % (2**30 - 1)

      # Translate the deterministic order into times in the past, so that records
      # created during test runs are also always newer than the fixtures.
      base_time = Time.utc(2024, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0)
      timestamp = base_time + (fixture_int / 1000.0)

      uuid_v7_with_timestamp(timestamp, label)
    end

    def uuid_v7_with_timestamp(time, seed_string)
      # Generate UUIDv7 with custom timestamp and deterministic random bits
      # Format: 48-bit timestamp_ms | 12-bit sub_ms_precision | 4-bit version | 62-bit random

      time_ms = time.to_f * 1000
      timestamp_ms = time_ms.to_i

      # 48-bit timestamp (milliseconds since epoch)
      bytes = []
      bytes[0] = (timestamp_ms >> 40) & 0xff
      bytes[1] = (timestamp_ms >> 32) & 0xff
      bytes[2] = (timestamp_ms >> 24) & 0xff
      bytes[3] = (timestamp_ms >> 16) & 0xff
      bytes[4] = (timestamp_ms >> 8) & 0xff
      bytes[5] = timestamp_ms & 0xff

      # Use the 12-bit rand_a field for sub-millisecond precision
      # Extract fractional milliseconds and convert to 12-bit value (0-4095)
      # This gives us ~0.244 microsecond precision
      frac_ms = time_ms - timestamp_ms
      sub_ms_precision = (frac_ms * 4096).to_i & 0xfff

      # Derive deterministic "random" bits from seed_string for the remaining random bits
      hash = Digest::MD5.hexdigest(seed_string)

      # 12-bit sub-ms precision + 4-bit version (0111 for v7)
      bytes[6] = ((sub_ms_precision >> 8) & 0x0f) | 0x70  # version 7
      bytes[7] = sub_ms_precision & 0xff

      # 2-bit variant (10) + 62-bit random
      rand_b = hash[3...19].to_i(16) & ((2**62) - 1)
      bytes[8] = ((rand_b >> 56) & 0x3f) | 0x80  # variant 10
      bytes[9] = (rand_b >> 48) & 0xff
      bytes[10] = (rand_b >> 40) & 0xff
      bytes[11] = (rand_b >> 32) & 0xff
      bytes[12] = (rand_b >> 24) & 0xff
      bytes[13] = (rand_b >> 16) & 0xff
      bytes[14] = (rand_b >> 8) & 0xff

# Fix for SQLite FTS5 virtual table schema dumping
# Rails has a bug where it doesn't handle FTS5 content= and content_rowid= options

module SQLiteFTS5SchemaDumperFix
  # Override the virtual_tables method to handle FTS5 syntax properly
  def virtual_tables(stream)
    # Query sqlite_master for all virtual tables
    virtual_table_sqls = @connection.select_rows(
      "SELECT name, sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table' AND sql LIKE 'CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE%'"
    )

    virtual_table_sqls.each do |table_name, sql|
      # Just output the raw SQL since create_virtual_table doesn't handle our syntax
      stream.puts "  execute #{sql.inspect}"
      stream.puts
    end
  end
end

ActiveSupport.on_load(:active_record_sqlite3adapter) do
  ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::SQLite3::SchemaDumper.prepend(SQLiteFTS5SchemaDumperFix)

step() {

  # mise meets the floor — and the shim dir is configurable, so probe by running
  # gum rather than matching paths. Any failure falls back to plain echo.
  if gum --version &> /dev/null; then
    gum style --foreground 135 --bold "▸ $step_name"
    gum style --foreground 240 "$*"
  else
    echo "▸ $step_name"
    echo "$*"
  fi

  "$@"

  local exit_code=$?
  echo
  return $exit_code
}

mise_min_version="2026.7.10" # keep in lockstep with min_version in .mise.toml

mise_too_old() {
  local current="$(mise --version 2>/dev/null | awk '{ print $1; exit }')"
  [ "$(printf '%s\n' "$mise_min_version" "$current" | sort -V | head -1)" != "$mise_min_version" ]

ensure_correct_mise_install() {
  if ! command -v mise &> /dev/null; then
    # brew installs are a macOS decision — a Linuxbrew host must not gain a
    # brew-owned mise moments before the manager gate rejects or ignores it
    if [ "$(uname -s)" = Darwin ] && command -v brew &> /dev/null; then
      # refresh the formula index first: a stale one (fresh VM images, long-idle
      # machines) resolves an old mise and the version floor is unreachable
      brew update --quiet || true
      brew install mise
    elif command -v pacman &> /dev/null; then
      sudo pacman -S --noconfirm --needed mise
    else

      exit 1

    # Upgrade the ACTIVE mise, classified by the resolved binary's owner — a brew
    # keg can coexist with the pacman/dpkg/mise.run install PATH actually
    # resolves, and upgrading an inactive copy would leave the floor unmet.
    mise_path="$(readlink -f "$(command -v mise)")"

      # long-idle machines) brew considers an old mise current and this upgrade

module FixturesTestHelper
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  class_methods do
    def identify(label, column_type = :integer)
      if label.to_s.end_with?("_uuid")
        column_type = :uuid
        label = label.to_s.delete_suffix("_uuid")
      end

      # Rails passes :string for varchar columns, so handle both :uuid and :string
      return super(label, column_type) unless column_type.in?([ :uuid, :string ])
      generate_fixture_uuid(label)
    end

    private

    def generate_fixture_uuid(label)
      # Generate deterministic UUIDv7 for fixtures that sorts by fixture ID
      # This allows .first/.last to work as expected in tests
      # Use the same CRC32 algorithm as Rails' default fixture ID generation
      # so that UUIDs sort in the same order as integer IDs
      fixture_int = Zlib.crc32("fixtures/#{label}") % (2**30 - 1)

      # Translate the deterministic order into times in the past, so that records
      # created during test runs are also always newer than the fixtures.
      base_time = Time.utc(2024, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0)
      timestamp = base_time + (fixture_int / 1000.0)

      uuid_v7_with_timestamp(timestamp, label)
    end

    def uuid_v7_with_timestamp(time, seed_string)
      # Generate UUIDv7 with custom timestamp and deterministic random bits
      # Format: 48-bit timestamp_ms | 12-bit sub_ms_precision | 4-bit version | 62-bit random

      time_ms = time.to_f * 1000
      timestamp_ms = time_ms.to_i

      # 48-bit timestamp (milliseconds since epoch)
      bytes = []
      bytes[0] = (timestamp_ms >> 40) & 0xff
      bytes[1] = (timestamp_ms >> 32) & 0xff
      bytes[2] = (timestamp_ms >> 24) & 0xff
      bytes[3] = (timestamp_ms >> 16) & 0xff
      bytes[4] = (timestamp_ms >> 8) & 0xff
      bytes[5] = timestamp_ms & 0xff

      # Use the 12-bit rand_a field for sub-millisecond precision
      # Extract fractional milliseconds and convert to 12-bit value (0-4095)
      # This gives us ~0.244 microsecond precision
      frac_ms = time_ms - timestamp_ms
      sub_ms_precision = (frac_ms * 4096).to_i & 0xfff

      # Derive deterministic "random" bits from seed_string for the remaining random bits
      hash = Digest::MD5.hexdigest(seed_string)

      # 12-bit sub-ms precision + 4-bit version (0111 for v7)
      bytes[6] = ((sub_ms_precision >> 8) & 0x0f) | 0x70  # version 7
      bytes[7] = sub_ms_precision & 0xff

      # 2-bit variant (10) + 62-bit random
      rand_b = hash[3...19].to_i(16) & ((2**62) - 1)
      bytes[8] = ((rand_b >> 56) & 0x3f) | 0x80  # variant 10
      bytes[9] = (rand_b >> 48) & 0xff
      bytes[10] = (rand_b >> 40) & 0xff
      bytes[11] = (rand_b >> 32) & 0xff
      bytes[12] = (rand_b >> 24) & 0xff
      bytes[13] = (rand_b >> 16) & 0xff
      bytes[14] = (rand_b >> 8) & 0xff
      bytes[15] = rand_b & 0xff

      # Format as UUID string and convert to base36 (25 chars)
      uuid = "%02x%02x%02x%02x-%02x%02x-%02x%02x-%02x%02x-%02x%02x%02x%02x%02x%02x" % bytes

module SessionTestHelper
  def parsed_cookies
    ActionDispatch::Cookies::CookieJar.build(request, cookies.to_hash)
  end

  def sign_in_as(identity)
    cookies.delete :session_token

    if identity.is_a?(User)
      user = identity
      identity = user.identity
      raise "User #{user.name} (#{user.id}) doesn't have an associated identity" unless identity
    elsif !identity.is_a?(Identity)
      identity = identities(identity)
    end

    identity.send_magic_link
    magic_link = identity.magic_links.order(id: :desc).first

    untenanted do
      post session_path, params: { email_address: identity.email_address }
      post session_magic_link_url, params: { code: magic_link.code }
    end

    assert_response :redirect, "Posting the Magic Link code should grant access"

    cookie = cookies.get_cookie "session_token"
    assert_not_nil cookie, "Expected session_token cookie to be set after sign in"
  end

  def logout_and_sign_in_as(identity)
    Session.delete_all
    sign_in_as identity
  end

  def sign_out
    untenanted do
      delete session_path
    end
    assert_not cookies[:session_token].present?
  end

  def with_current_user(user)
    user = users(user) unless user.is_a? User
    @old_session = Current.session
    begin
      Current.session = Session.new(identity: user.identity)
      yield
    ensure
      Current.session = @old_session
    end
  end

  def untenanted(&block)
    original_script_name = integration_session.default_url_options[:script_name]
    integration_session.default_url_options[:script_name] = ""
    yield
  ensure
    integration_session.default_url_options[:script_name] = original_script_name
  end

  def with_multi_tenant_mode(enabled)
    previous = Account.multi_tenant
    Account.multi_tenant = enabled
    yield
  ensure
    Account.multi_tenant = previous
  end
end

require "test_helper"

class SignupTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  test "validates email format for identity creation" do
    signup = Signup.new(email_address: "not-an-email")
    assert_not signup.valid?(:identity_creation)
    assert signup.errors[:email_address].any?

    signup = Signup.new(email_address: "valid@example.com")
    assert signup.valid?(:identity_creation)
  end

  test "#create_identity" do
    signup = Signup.new(email_address: "brian@example.com")

    magic_link = nil
    assert_difference -> { Identity.count }, 1 do
      assert_difference -> { MagicLink.count }, 1 do
        magic_link = signup.create_identity
      end
    end

    assert_kind_of MagicLink, magic_link
    assert_empty signup.errors
    assert signup.identity
    assert signup.identity.persisted?

    signup_existing = Signup.new(email_address: "brian@example.com")

    assert_no_difference -> { Identity.count } do
      assert_difference -> { MagicLink.count }, 1 do
        magic_link = signup_existing.create_identity
      end
    end

    assert_kind_of MagicLink, magic_link

    signup_invalid = Signup.new(email_address: "")
    assert_raises do
      signup_invalid.create_identity
    end
  end

  test "#complete" do
    Account.any_instance.expects(:setup_customer_template).once

    Current.without_account do
      signup = Signup.new(full_name: "Kevin", identity: identities(:kevin))

      assert signup.complete

      assert signup.account
      assert signup.user
      assert_equal "Kevin", signup.user.name

      signup_invalid = Signup.new(
        full_name: "",
        identity: identities(:kevin)
      )
      assert_not signup_invalid.complete
      assert_not_empty signup_invalid.errors[:full_name]
    end
  end

  test "#complete with invalid data" do
    Current.without_account do
      signup = Signup.new
      assert_not signup.complete
      assert signup.errors[:full_name].any?
      assert signup.errors[:identity].any?
      assert_nil signup.account
      assert_nil signup.user
    end
  end

  test "#complete with name that is too long" do
    Current.without_account do
      signup = Signup.new(full_name: "A" * 241, identity: identities(:kevin))
      signup.expects(:create_tenant).never

      assert_not signup.complete

      assert signup.errors[:full_name].any?
      assert_nil signup.account
      assert_nil signup.user
    end
  end
end

messages.thinking:
**Deep Dive into Export/Import Architecture**

Okay, let's get down to brass tacks. We've got a comprehensive grasp of the codebase now, and it's time to meticulously dissect every requirement and existing architectural element.  We're dealing with *two* export types and *one* import functionality. The primary focus should be on how we can implement and integrate these features effectively.

**Understanding the Requirements:**

We have to meet the needs of a major client. I've re-read the prompt and the `AGENTS.md` documentation, which lays out the core requirements for data export and import.  Specifically, we need to handle both local and S3 storage, deal with *massive* ZIP files (up to 500GB!), and leverage existing models like those in `app/models/account/data_transfer/`.

*   **Export Type 1:** The "Account Export" initiated by an admin from Account Settings. This generates a `.zip` containing the *entire* account data (boards, cards, comments, files, users, etc.). It appears that `Account::DataTransfer::Manifest`, `RecordSet`s, and `ZipFile` are the current key components. We should note that we already have the basic infrastructure for data transfer here. It's essentially a comprehensive account backup. This export will be brought back in at `/account/imports/new` to create a new account with the full data transfer.

    A key question is how the records will be stored in this file. The `Account::DataTransfer::Manifest` is crucial. The manifest already lists many of the main models in the system, but we need to check how it actually writes and reads the files. Are individual records/batches serialized to JSON/files or is it a database dump?

    An important point is that `Account::DataTransfer::RecordSet` indicates the concept of `INTERNAL_RECORD_TYPES`. It is highly likely that there is an existing `Export` class that manages all exports (account, user). ActiveStorage will be using the `Export` base class (or STI child classes) to store exported files. Let's make sure that imported files are properly excluded, and/or purged, during export.

*   **Export Type 2:** The "User / Profile Export" is simpler. Any signed-in user can download *their* visible cards. Importantly, these exports should be accessible from the user's profile page, which will require a UI change.  The `.zip` will contain cards as JSON along with associated comments, attachments, and images.

*   **Import:**  The import functionality works on the `/account/imports/new` endpoint. It needs to handle a `.zip` file and reconstruct a full account.  An import that can't be completed leaves nothing behind.  We need to carefully consider how we roll back failed imports. We'll need to email notifications for success and failure.

**Detailed Analysis of Existing Code:**

The discovery of the `INTERNAL_RECORD_TYPES` constant within `RecordSet` is a critical piece of the puzzle.  It strongly suggests a polymorphic association with an `Export` model (or STI subclasses like `Account::Export` and `User::DataExport`). ActiveStorage stores `record_type` as `Export` for the attached files of the exports (even if subclasses). We need to verify that our import process excludes these export attachments.  It's crucial to prevent exports from potentially re-exporting the import file. Thus the import's `.zip` would become part of the export, increasing the size of each successive export.

Given that we are aiming for very large files, it is likely that we want to save data in a format other than database dumps. We can use a combination of JSON files stored along with images, videos, and other assets.

We will also need to review `ExportMailer`, `ImportMailer` or any existing mailing code that handles asynchronous jobs. We must also check existing code in Fizzy and other 37signals apps to identify established conventions and design patterns for exports and imports.

# Fizzy

This is the source code of [Fizzy](https://fizzy.do/), the Kanban tracking tool for issues and ideas by [37signals](https://37signals.com).


## Running your own Fizzy instance

If you want to run your own Fizzy instance, but don't need to change its code, you can use our pre-built Docker image.
You'll need access to a server on which you can run Docker, and you'll need to configure some options to customize your installation.

You can find the details of how to do a Docker-based deployment in our [Docker deployment guide](docs/docker-deployment.md).

If you want more flexibility to customize your Fizzy installation by changing its code, and deploy those changes to your server, then we recommend you deploy Fizzy with Kamal. You can find a complete walkthrough of doing that in our [Kamal deployment guide](docs/kamal-deployment.md).


## Development

You are welcome -- and encouraged -- to modify Fizzy to your liking.
Please see our [Development guide](docs/development.md) for how to get Fizzy set up for local development.


## Contributing

We welcome contributions! Please read our [style guide](STYLE.md) before submitting code.


## License

Fizzy is released under the [O'Saasy License](LICENSE.md).

messages.thinking:
**Deep Dive into System Design: Export Functionality**

Okay, here's the plan. I need to nail this export system, meeting every requirement with absolute precision while staying true to the codebase's established style and existing infrastructure. This is what I'm thinking:

First, understanding the requirements is key. The user, as an admin, should be able to download the entire account as a .zip, accessible from Account Settings. Any user can download their visible cards from their profile. The user receives an email with a time-limited download link. So, I need to design this piece by piece.

*   **Account Settings and Route Planning:** We know the account settings route is at `/account/settings`. Now, I need to add a way for the admin to initiate a full account export. The `config/routes.rb` reveals the `account` namespace, and it has an `exports` resource that supports `create` and `show`. The create action will be the start of an export, and the show action will likely be used after the email is delivered.
*   **Export Workflow:** The `account/exports#create` controller action will need to create an `Account::Export` record and kick off a background job to build the .zip. The user needs to be redirected to the account settings with a flash message to indicate the download is in progress. The background job will handle the heavy lifting of gathering all the data, zipping it up, and storing the archive.
*   **The Download Link Conundrum:** The email will contain the download link. The critical question: should `account/exports#show` *redirect* to the zip file, or *render* a page with a download link? Thinking this through, I realize "the link works for a day" is crucial. This means the link should be time-limited. If it's a redirect, it simplifies the click-and-download process. But if it renders a download page, that gives us the flexibility to validate the link's expiry and give a message to the user when it expires. For an integration test, I must consider the scenarios to handle: If I make the assumption that it immediately starts the download, the tests may fail.
*   **Security and Expiration:**  For the link to expire, I can't rely on `rails_blob_url` alone. I have to make the link point to a controller action (like `account/exports#show`) that checks the `export` record's expiry before serving the file. This way, even if the file is stored with a permanent URL, the controller can enforce the one-day limit.
*   **Edge Cases and Tests:**  I need to consider all edge cases: rate limiting, concurrent exports, and invalid links. I need a robust system of tests. I'll need system tests that simulate users clicking the link in the email and ensure the download works *and* that it expires.
*   **Implementation:** I will now use `ZipFile` with `ZipFile::Writer` and other existing classes. The zip file should be created using Active Storage, possibly with streaming to handle large archives efficiently. I'll re-read existing mailers and controllers to make sure my implementation integrates seamlessly with the existing structure.

messages.thinking:
**Analyzing Data Export Design Options**

Okay, let's break this down. The core functionality involves allowing admins to download the entire account data, and users to download their individual card data, all within a time-limited window. The system uses emails with download links, so let's carefully compare the two options for handling these links and their associated pages.

First, the process starts with an admin initiating an export via the account settings or a user via their profile page. This triggers either `Account::Export` or `User::DataExport` (both inheriting from a base `Export` class).  Jobs are enqueued to build these exports, and the user is notified. Once the export is complete, the status is updated, and an email is sent. The critical thing here is the link within that email.

For an `Account::Export`, the link will be of the form `account_export_url(export)`, while for `User::DataExport` it will be `user_data_export_url(export.user, export)`.  Now, the crux: what happens when that link is clicked or visited.

We have two design options:

1.  **Design 1:**  A `GET .../exports/:id` request renders a `show.html.erb` download page. This page shows a "Download your data" button (or a simple link) that points to `rails_blob_path(@export.file, disposition: :attachment)`. The page would handle the expired state (after a day).
2.  **Design 2:** A `GET .../exports/:id` request *directly* redirects to `rails_blob_path(@export.file, disposition: :attachment)`.  Expiration or absence is handled by returning a 404/410 status.

The crucial constraint is the "link works for a day" requirement. So let's look at Design 2. If a user clicks the email link, and they're not signed in, the authentication flow saves the current URL for a redirect. Once logged in, the system redirects to `GET .../exports/:id` which then *immediately* triggers the download, fulfilling the "download link" part. Crucially, the system needs to check if the link is still valid.  If it's clicked after a day, then `GET .../exports/:id` should detect `@export.expired?` and return a 404 or 410.  The same is true for the Active Storage `rails_blob_path` link itself.

This is where the ActiveStorage authorization comes in. When the `rails_blob_path` is accessed, the code checks `@blob.accessible_to?(Current.user)`. This gets translated to `@export.accessible_to?(Current.user)`, which needs to return `true` only if the user is present and the export belongs to them. For `Account::Export`, it needs to check the user is an admin.  Critically, it needs to check if the export is both completed and has not expired.  This means that the *ActiveStorage* path itself becomes time-limited, which is perfect and efficient.

However, consider the *show page*. If a user starts an export and gets an email, then it's essential to understand the UX flow. If they *return* to the site and click a link there, what should happen? The email could link to `account_export_url(@export)` (or a similar URL). When a user then `GET /account/exports/:id` do we want to render a page ("Your export is ready" with a download link) or simply redirect?  The Basecamp/HEY/Fizzy style guide is helpful here. A direct redirect (Design 2B) is the more direct and elegant solution, as it gets the user to their download, while still allowing the system to handle the expired/404 cases.

  CODE_LENGTH = 6
  EXPIRATION_TIME = 15.minutes

  belongs_to :identity

  enum :purpose, %w[ sign_in sign_up ], prefix: :for, default: :sign_in

  scope :active, -> { where(expires_at: Time.current...) }
  scope :stale, -> { where(expires_at: ..Time.current) }

  before_validation :generate_code, on: :create
  before_validation :set_expiration, on: :create

  validates :code, uniqueness: true, presence: true

  class << self
    def consume(code)
      active.find_by(code: Code.sanitize(code))&.consume
    end

    def cleanup
      stale.delete_all
    end
  end

  def consume
    destroy
    self
  end

  private
    def generate_code
      self.code ||= loop do
        candidate = Code.generate(CODE_LENGTH)
        break candidate unless self.class.exists?(code: candidate)
      end
    end

    def set_expiration
      self.expires_at ||= EXPIRATION_TIME.from_now
    end
end

class Webhook::Delivery < ApplicationRecord
  include Rails.application.routes.url_helpers

  class ResponseTooLarge < StandardError; end

  STALE_TRESHOLD = 7.days
  USER_AGENT = "fizzy/1.0.0 Webhook"
  ENDPOINT_TIMEOUT = 7.seconds
  MAX_RESPONSE_SIZE = 100.kilobytes

  belongs_to :account, default: -> { webhook.account }
  belongs_to :webhook
  belongs_to :event

  store :request, coder: JSON
  store :response, coder: JSON

  enum :state, %w[ pending in_progress completed errored ].index_by(&:itself), default: :pending

  scope :ordered, -> { order created_at: :desc, id: :desc }
  scope :stale, -> { where(created_at: ...STALE_TRESHOLD.ago) }

  after_create_commit :deliver_later

  def self.cleanup(batch_size: 500, pause: 0.1)
    sleep pause until stale.limit(batch_size).delete_all.zero?
  end

  def deliver_later
    Webhook::DeliveryJob.perform_later(self)
  end

  def deliver
    in_progress!

    self.request[:headers] = headers
    self.response = perform_request
    self.state = :completed
    save!

    webhook.delinquency_tracker.record_delivery_of(self)
  rescue
    errored!
    raise
  end

  def sanitized_request
    if headers = request&.dig("headers")&.except("X-Webhook-Signature")
      { headers: headers }
    end
  end

  def response_summary
    if response.present?
      { code: response[:code], error: response[:error] }
    end
  end

  def failed?
    (errored? || completed?) && !succeeded?
  end

  def succeeded?
    completed? && response[:error].blank? && response[:code].between?(200, 299)
  end

  private
    def perform_request
      if resolved_ip.nil?
        { error: :private_uri }

require "stringio"

# A very barebones ZIP file reader. Is made for maximum interoperability, but at the same
# time we attempt to keep it somewhat concise.
#
# ## REALLY CRAZY IMPORTANT STUFF: SECURITY IMPLICATIONS
#
# Please **BEWARE** - using this is a security risk if you are reading files that have been
# supplied by users. This implementation has _not_ been formally verified for correctness. As
# ZIP files contain relative offsets in lots of places it might be possible for a maliciously
# crafted ZIP file to put the decode procedure in an endless loop, make it attempt huge reads
# from the input file and so on. Additionally, the reader module for deflated data has
# no support for ZIP bomb protection. So either limit the `FileReader` usage to the files you
# trust, or triple-check all the inputs upfront. Patches to make this reader more secure
# are welcome of course.
#
# ## Usage
#
#     File.open('zipfile.zip', 'rb') do |f|
#       entries = ZipKit::FileReader.read_zip_structure(io: f)
#       entries.each do |e|
#         File.open(e.filename, 'wb') do |extracted_file|
#           ex = e.extractor_from(f)
#           extracted_file << ex.extract(1024 * 1024) until ex.eof?
#         end
#       end
#     end
#
# ## Supported features
#
# * Deflate and stored storage modes
# * Zip64 (extra fields and offsets)
# * Data descriptors
#
# ## Unsupported features
#
# * Archives split over multiple disks/files
# * Any ZIP encryption
# * EFS language flag and InfoZIP filename extra field
# * CRC32 checksums are _not_ verified
#
# ## Mode of operation
#
# By default, `FileReader` _ignores_ the data in local file headers (as it is
# often unreliable). It reads the ZIP file "from the tail", finds the
# end-of-central-directory signatures, then reads the central directory entries,
# reconstitutes the entries with their filenames, attributes and so on, and
# sets these entries up with the absolute _offsets_ into the source file/IO object.
# These offsets can then be used to extract the actual compressed data of
# the files and to expand it.
#
# ## Recovering damaged or incomplete ZIP files
#
# If the ZIP file you are trying to read does not contain the central directory
# records `read_zip_structure` will not work, since it starts the read process
# from the EOCD marker at the end of the central directory and then crawls
# "back" in the IO to figure out the rest. You can explicitly apply a fallback
# for reading the archive "straight ahead" instead using `read_zip_straight_ahead`
# - the method will instead scan your IO from the very start, skipping over
# the actual entry data. This is less efficient than central directory parsing since
# it involves a much larger number of reads (1 read from the IO per entry in the ZIP).

class ZipKit::FileReader::InflatingReader
  def initialize(from_io, compressed_data_size)
    @io = from_io
    @compressed_data_size = compressed_data_size
    @already_read = 0
    @zlib_inflater = ::Zlib::Inflate.new(-Zlib::MAX_WBITS)
  end

  def extract(n_bytes = nil)
    n_bytes ||= (@compressed_data_size - @already_read)

    return if eof?

    available = @compressed_data_size - @already_read

    return if available.zero?

    n_bytes = available if n_bytes > available

    return "" if n_bytes.zero?

    compressed_chunk = @io.read(n_bytes)

    return if compressed_chunk.nil?

    @already_read += compressed_chunk.bytesize
    @zlib_inflater.inflate(compressed_chunk)
  end

  def eof?
    @zlib_inflater.finished?
  end
end

# Is used to write ZIP archives without having to read them back or to overwrite
# data. It outputs into any object that supports `<<` or `write`, namely:
#
# * `Array` - will contain binary strings
# * `File` - data will be written to it as it gets generated
# * `IO` (`Socket`, `StringIO`) - data gets written into it
# * `String` - in binary encoding and unfrozen - also makes a decent output target
#
# or anything else that responds to `#<<` or `#write`.
#
# You can also combine output through the `Streamer` with direct output to the destination,
# all while preserving the correct offsets in the ZIP file structures. This allows usage
# of `sendfile()` or socket `splice()` calls for "through" proxying.
#
# If you want to avoid data descriptors - or write data bypassing the Streamer -
# you need to know the CRC32 (as a uint) and the filesize upfront,
# before the writing of the entry body starts.
#
# ## Using the Streamer with runtime compression
#
# You can use the Streamer with data descriptors (the CRC32 and the sizes will be
# written after the file data). This allows non-rewinding on-the-fly compression.
# The streamer will pick the optimum compression method ("stored" or "deflated")
# depending on the nature of the byte stream you send into it (by using a small buffer).
# If you are compressing large files, the Deflater object that the Streamer controls
# will be regularly flushed to prevent memory inflation.
#
#     ZipKit::Streamer.open(file_socket_or_string) do |zip|
#       zip.write_file('mov.mp4') do |sink|
#         File.open('mov.mp4', 'rb'){|source| IO.copy_stream(source, sink) }
#       end
#       zip.write_file('long-novel.txt') do |sink|
#         File.open('novel.txt', 'rb'){|source| IO.copy_stream(source, sink) }
#       end
#     end
#
# The central directory will be written automatically at the end of the `open` block.
#
# ## Using the Streamer with entries of known size and having a known CRC32 checksum
#
# Streamer allows "IO splicing" - in this mode it will only control the metadata output,
# but you can write the data to the socket/file outside of the Streamer. For example, when
# using the sendfile gem:
#
#     ZipKit::Streamer.open(socket) do | zip |
#       zip.add_stored_entry(filename: "myfile1.bin", size: 9090821, crc32: 12485)
#       socket.sendfile(tempfile1)
#       zip.simulate_write(tempfile1.size)
#
#       zip.add_stored_entry(filename: "myfile2.bin", size: 458678, crc32: 89568)
#       socket.sendfile(tempfile2)
#       zip.simulate_write(tempfile2.size)
#     end
#
# Note that you need to use `simulate_write` in this case. This needs to happen since Streamer
# writes absolute offsets into the ZIP (local file header offsets and the like),
# and it relies on the output object to tell it how many bytes have been written
# so far. When using `sendfile` the Ruby write methods get bypassed entirely, and the
# offsets in the IO will not be updated - which will result in an invalid ZIP.
#
#
# ## On-the-fly deflate -using the Streamer with async/suspended writes and data descriptors
#
# If you are unable to use the block versions of `write_deflated_file` and `write_stored_file`
# there is an option to use a separate writer object. It gets returned from `write_deflated_file`
# and `write_stored_file` if you do not provide them with a block, and will accept data writes.
# Do note that you _must_ call `#close` on that object yourself:
#
#     ZipKit::Streamer.open(socket) do | zip |
#       w = zip.write_stored_file('mov.mp4')
#       IO.copy_stream(source_io, w)
#       w.close
#     end
#
# The central directory will be written automatically at the end of the `open` block. If you need
# to manage the Streamer manually, or defer the central directory write until appropriate, use
# the constructor instead and call `Streamer#close`:
#
#     zip = ZipKit::Streamer.new(out_io)
#     .....
#     zip.close
#
# Calling {Streamer#close} **will not** call `#close` on the underlying IO object.
class ZipKit::Streamer
  autoload :DeflatedWriter, File.dirname(__FILE__) + "/streamer/deflated_writer.rb"
  autoload :Writable, File.dirname(__FILE__) + "/streamer/writable.rb"

messages.content: Let's inspect how `ActionText::RichText` stores attachments, blobs, and user `@mentions` in `body` HTML across `app/` and `test/`.
messages.thinking:
**Deep Dive into Account Import and Data Integrity**

Okay, let's break this down. We need to be *extremely* careful when importing account data, especially concerning primary keys (`id`) and unique indexes. My primary concern is the potential for collisions and data corruption in *both* scenarios – importing to a new instance and importing back into the same instance, particularly when the original account still exists.

First, I need to understand the data structure: Every table in `Manifest` has a `t.uuid` which is the `id`, a globally unique primary key. And then we have those critical unique indexes on key fields like `external_account_id`, `key` in `active_storage_blobs`, and `key` in `board_publications`.

**Scenario 1 (Importing to a new instance):** Here, we're likely safe, as the UUIDs from Instance 1 won't exist in Instance 2, except for `external_account_id`, which might clash if the new instance is already using sequential IDs.

**Scenario 2 (Importing back into the same instance *while the account already exists*):** This is where it gets hairy. The prompt states the user can import a file and get a new account with the *same* data. If we kept the old IDs (UUIDs), blob keys, and board publication keys, importing would *immediately* fail due to `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique` errors (primary key/unique key collisions). Worse, if ActiveStorage blobs had the same key, deleting a blob in the *new* account would accidentally delete the original file on disk or S3! That's a disaster.

This brings me to the very important purpose of the `Account::DataTransfer::` subclasses of `RecordSet` defined in `Manifest`:

1.  `AccountRecordSet`
2.  `UserRecordSet`
3.  `EntropyRecordSet`
4.  `ActiveStorage::BlobRecordSet`
5.  `ActiveStorage::AttachmentRecordSet`
6.  `ActiveStorage::FileRecordSet`
7.  `ActionText::RichTextRecordSet`

Why are *these* specific classes special, while `Board`, `Card`, `Comment`, etc. use the generic `RecordSet`? Looking at the code, it becomes clear:

*   **`EntropyRecordSet` is crucial:** Look at the `entropy` table! It's related to the `container_type` and `container_id` of accounts. When a new account is created, an `Entropy` record is automatically created for that account with a unique index. So `EntropyRecordSet` either updates `account.entropy` or remaps `container_id` for `"Account"` -> `account.id` to prevent conflicts.

*   **`AccountRecordSet`:** The new `Account` ALREADY EXISTS because it was created at the beginning of the import! So `AccountRecordSet` UPDATES the new `account` instead of inserting a second `Account` row!

*   **`ActionText::RichTextRecordSet`:** We NEED to know how it handles attachments! This is particularly important for things *inside* the `action_text_rich_texts.body` field (which might contain attachments through `sgid` or `@mentions`), so we need to inspect the contents of that column.

So, in summary, we're building this carefully to prevent collisions: The import system must be intelligently handling UUIDs and unique indexes to avoid data corruption and ensure the integrity of the data being imported. This is done through a well-designed `RecordSet` system that correctly remaps IDs and updates existing data in a safe way.

messages.thinking:
**The Data Import/Export Revelation**

Okay, I think I'm starting to grasp this. It's all clicking into place now. I was focusing on the wrong things initially, but after digging into `action_text_rich_texts.body` and `config/initializers/active_storage.rb`, a clearer picture is emerging.

The key lies in how ActionText attachments and ActiveStorage blobs are handled during an export and import.  Specifically, it seems `sgid` is a **Signed GlobalID**, and it's signed with the originating server's `secret_key_base`.  When data moves between Fizzy instances with *different* `secret_key_base` values, that signature becomes invalid. This explains why the export process doesn't rely on it.

Instead, the `ActionText::RichTextRecordSet` on export cleverly replaces the `sgid` in `<action-text-attachment>` with a `gid`. This is the plain attachable's Global ID, like `gid://fizzy/ActiveStorage::Blob/...`.  The `url` attribute within the `action-text-attachment` becomes a relative path, constructed via `polymorphic_url` from `config/initializers/active_storage.rb`. It's a lifesaver, ensuring portability across environments by including the `Current.account&.slug`.

The content of `action_text_rich_texts.body` now makes complete sense: it contains the original server's signed `sgid` and  a relative `url` that points to resources.

Critically, the order of the `RecordSet` instances within `Manifest` is crucial. The `UserRecordSet`, `BlobRecordSet`, `VariantRecord`, and `AttachmentRecordSet` have to run *before* `ActionText::RichTextRecordSet`.  This is because at the time `ActionText::RichTextRecordSet` is running, all users and blobs *already* exist in the target database.  This enables the system to locate the imported `User` / `ActiveStorage::Blob`, generate a fresh `attachable_sgid` with the *importing instance's* `secret_key_base`, and update the `url` using `polymorphic_url`, this time with the new account's slug. It's genius. And then ActiveStorage uploads the actual files.  It's all so elegantly orchestrated!

**UUID Collision and Deterministic Mapping**

Now, the UUID questions are the next critical problem to tackle. With `Board`, `Column`, `Card`, etc, all using the same `Account::DataTransfer::RecordSet`, I see the potential for disaster.  If a customer imports a backup *into the same instance*, we *will* have primary key collisions. I can imagine the customer service calls, already! The `id` values of every single table—`users`, `user_settings`, `tags`, `boards`, `columns`, `entropies`, `board_publications`, `webhooks`, `accesses`, `cards`, `comments`, `steps`, `assignments`, `taggings`, `closures`, `card_goldnesses`, `card_not_nows`, `card_activity_spikes`, `watches`, `pins`, `reactions`, `mentions`, `filters`, `events`, `notifications`, `notification_bundles`, `webhook_deliveries`, `active_storage_blobs`, `active_storage_variant_records`, `active_storage_attachments`, `action_text_rich_texts`—would conflict if they try to reuse the same IDs!

We *must* remap UUIDs. I'm thinking deterministic mappings or an ID map is the only solution. The goal is to ensure:
1.  Imports to different servers work without issue.
2.  Imports to the *same* server (multiple times, even!) are collision-free and preserve UUIDv7 time ordering.

I need to read `lib/rails_ext/active_record_uuid_type.rb` to understand how UUIDv7 works in the current context. Then, I need to figure out how we can create a UUID mapping algorithm to ensure the same object always gets the same mapped UUID, while maintaining time-based ordering.

messages.thinking:
**Deterministic UUIDv7 Remapping for Data Migrations**

Okay, stop and think about this for a moment – deterministic, order-preserving UUIDv7 remapping. This is elegant. Let's break down the UUIDv7 math. It's a 128-bit structure, effectively a 25-character base36 string. The crucial part for sorting is the first 64 bits: timestamp, version (7), and sub-millisecond precision. This is what guarantees that chronological order is maintained during the import, which is critical for operations like `.first`, `.last`, and chronologically ordered queries (e.g., `Comment.chronologically` or `Storage::Entry`). The remaining 64 bits are for variant and randomness.

Now, imagine a pure function, `remap_id(old_uuid, seed: new_account.id)`. Here's the core:

*   If `old_uuid` matches the old account ID, we simply return the new account's ID.
*   For any other UUID (except for `Identity` as it's global), we do this: we convert the UUID to hex, and **keep the first 16 hex characters (the timestamp, sub-ms order, and version) identical**. Then we compute a SHA256 digest using the new account ID and the old UUID.  The bottom 62 bits of this SHA256 digest (with variant set to "10") are used as the new random component. Finally, it's converted back to base36.

**Crucially, verify every property of this pure function:**

1.  **Zero RAM Overhead:** This works perfectly with huge archives! No need for massive in-memory lookup tables. It's O(1) CPU and O(1) memory, deterministic, and efficient for the whole import!
2.  **100% Referential Integrity:** Every UUID column in the database (determined via `model.columns_hash` and `column.type == :uuid`) is remapped this way.  Even within JSON columns, HABTM tables, and `ActionText::RichText` GIDs, everything is consistently mapped.  `Identity` is correctly resolved by email.
3.  **100% Preservation of Sort Order:** Because the leading 64 bits are identical, the sort order is flawlessly maintained after remapping, just as the original archive was sorted.
4.  **Zero Collisions:** Importing into the same Fizzy instance multiple times (even the same `.zip` multiple times) will not result in any collisions due to the new account ID being a brand-new UUIDv7 for every import with an extremely large random namespace.
5.  **`ActiveStorage::Blob#key` and `Board::Publication#key`:** Critical for unique filenames/keys on disk or S3.
    *   Since these `key` values are unique in the database and represent the filenames.  If not remapped, importing the same `.zip` twice will cause unique index violations!
    *   Also, deleting an account would delete the *original* file.
    *   A deterministic new `blob.key` is created (e.g., a SHA256-based key based on the new account ID) is generated and associated with the `ActiveStorage::Blob`.
    *   During the import, `FileRecordSet` reads from the original archive with the old key, and writes to storage with the new key.
    *   Cleanup/rollback during the import will never affect the original account's files.
    *   The same principle applies for `Board::Publication#key`, ensuring unique publishing keys.

I'm going to scan all the models in `Manifest`, looking at every column, type, association, and HABTM table now, just to be sure nothing gets missed. A `bin/rails runner` script will do the job.

messages.thinking:
**Importing Like a Boss: Strategic Data Migration**

Alright, let's break this down. First, I see an opportunity here. Inspecting these models, I've got a solid plan for data migration.

1.  **Filters:**
    The `Filter` model is interesting. It's got the usual JSON (`fields`) but also HABTM joins (`tags`, `boards`, `assignees`, `creators`, `closers`). This means if I properly handle those association IDs during the export/import or remap `card_ids` and `column_ids` in `fields`, the filters will work perfectly in the new environment. So either export the `tag_ids`, `board_ids`, etc, or remap the IDs of the `cards` and `columns` in the `fields` JSON.
2.  **Events:**
    For the `Event` model, the `particulars` field is JSON with `assignee_ids`, which are just User UUIDs. As long as those UUIDs are remapped during import, the event descriptions (like "Alice assigned this to Bob") will stay correct, that's key.
3.  **Callbacks: The Danger Zone!**
    Now, the biggest gotcha: those ActiveRecord callbacks! Let's think about this. Creating individual records (e.g., `Comment.create!` or `Card.create!`) during import triggers a cascade of unwanted side effects, which would also make the import slow.
    *   `Comment.create!` would generate redundant `Event` records, resulting in duplicated notifications and webhooks to external URLs.
    *   `Webhook.create!` would duplicate `Webhook::DelinquencyTracker` records.
    *   `User.create!` would create duplicate `User::Settings` and `Access` records (which can lead to unique index violations).
    *   `Card.create!` would cause the `account.cards_count` to be incremented and assign wrong `number`s.

    Essentially, it would take ages to insert a million records with all those callbacks active.

    **The Solution: `insert_all!` to the Rescue!**

    The approach I need to take is to use `model.insert_all!(batch)` with properly serialized attributes. This bypasses those callbacks, keeping the `created_at`, `updated_at`, `number`, etc., exact, and avoids all that unnecessary spam and potential conflicts. Plus, it's exponentially faster.

    **Post-Import Cleanup:**

    Once the data is imported, then I'll:

    1.  **Reindex the Search Index:** I need to reindex the searchable records (`Card` and `Comment`) in the new account to enable full-text search. Batch `insert_all` the records into `Search::Record.for(account.id)` or use `find_each(&:reindex)`. I'll need to check the `Search::Record` models (`sqlite.rb` and `trilogy.rb`) to understand how the search index is built, especially given SQLite FTS5 vs MySQL Trilogy search records.
    2.  **Reconcile Storage:** I'll need to run `account.reconcile_storage` and `account.boards.find_each(&:reconcile_storage)`, then follow it with `account.materialize_storage` and `account.boards.find_each(&:materialize_storage)`. This makes sure `Storage::Total` and `Storage::Entry` are consistent in the new account.

So, the plan is clear, now to examine the `app/models/search/record.rb`, `app/models/search/record/sqlite.rb`, `app/models/search/record/trilogy.rb`, `app/models/card/searchable.rb`, and `app/models/comment/searchable.rb` files to solidify the details. This is all about efficiency and data integrity.

**Deep Dive into User and Identity Management During Account Export/Import**

Okay, let's break this down. First, I need to ensure that after re-indexing `Card` and `Comment` objects, the full-text search works consistently, regardless of the database being SQLite or MySQL Trilogy. I see that the `reindex` method on the included records correctly triggers either `after_save :upsert_to_fts5_table` with integer IDs or `before_save :set_account_key, :stem_content` for the right shard, ensuring we're covered there.

Now, the core of this investigation: user and identity management during export and import. The prompt is clear: a signed-in user imports an account file, gets a new account with everything, and we're *not* leaving anything behind if the import fails.

Let's start by looking at `User` and `Identity` models in Fizzy.  I see the `identities` table with `id`, `email_address` (unique and normalized), and `staff` flags. The `users` table has the `account_id`, `identity_id` (crucially, *nullable* for the `system` user and deactivated users), `name`, `role`, `active` status, and `verified_at` with a unique index on `account_id` and `identity_id`.

I need to nail down the export process in `UserRecordSet#export`. What data do we *really* need to export for each `User`? Obviously, most of `User.column_names` like IDs, name, role, status are needed, but the *key* thing is: `identity_id` isn't meaningful across different instances, so just the `email_address` (from `user.identity&.email_address`) must be included! That's how we'll link users across Fizzy instances. We have to handle active users, system users (with `identity: nil`), and deactivated users (also `identity: nil`).

Now, what about the import process in `UserRecordSet#import`, and, *crucially*, what happens to the person who *initiates* the import, `importer_identity`? I've identified three scenarios:

*   **Case 1: `importer_identity` *was* already in the exported account (same email).** The `Identity.find_or_create_by!` method should find the existing `importer_identity`. But what if this user had a different role during the export (e.g. admin or member) or was the owner?  We need to make sure the user in the new account keeps their exact `User` record with all their associated data, and, if not, gets an `owner` / `admin` role or keep their current one.  Make sure `verified_at` is set.
*   **Case 2: `importer_identity` *was not* in the exported account.** This is where it gets interesting! If Bob imports an account file, and only `alice@acme.com` and `charlie@acme.com` are in the export, then Bob would have no access to the new account! That's a huge problem.
    To avoid this, we must ensure that all the original users from the exported file get imported (with `find_or_create_by!`) *and* that a `User` record is created/joined for `importer_identity` in the new account. This new user gets the `admin` role (or `owner` if no active owner exists), is verified, and gets their name from the identity or email.  We need to look at granting access to boards through `grant_access_to_boards`! Does `admin` automatically have access to all boards? We need to verify what `Board::Accessible` says.

        .joins("LEFT JOIN cards AS comment_cards ON comments.card_id = comment_cards.id")
        .where("(mentions.source_type = 'Card' AND cards.board_id = ?) OR (mentions.source_type = 'Comment' AND comment_cards.board_id = ?)", board_id_binary, board_id_binary)

      uuid_type = ActiveRecord::Type.lookup(:uuid, adapter: :trilogy)

    end

    def watches_for(user)

    end

    def pins_for(user)

**Deep Dive into Account Import Logic**

Okay, wow, that was a close call! I'm so glad we reviewed `Board::Accessible`. It's incredibly important that admins and owners are only seeing boards they *should* have access to. The `Access` record check is critical, ensuring security.

So, let's break down that import process, especially Case 2 where the importer isn't an exported user:

1.  **New User Creation and Access:** If Bob imports Alice's account, and Bob wasn't in the original export, we're creating a new user for Bob with `:owner` or `:admin` role. The system's logic ensures the importer gets at least administrator access. If they weren't in the exported user list, they get access to all the boards.

2.  **Access Granularity and Preservation:** It's smart how we ensure existing user permissions are exactly preserved. If Alice *was* in the export (like a re-import), her existing `Access` records remain intact, giving her the *same* board access she had before. This also works perfectly to ensure that if the importer *wasn't* in the exported account, the importer gets access to all boards in the new account! Even deactivated accounts are handled.

That `UNIQUE` index on `account_id` and `identity_id` on the `users` table is crucial for multiple `NULL` `identity_id` values which we *do* support. That's a good fail-safe.

Now, let's make 100% sure the other `RecordSet` classes are rock-solid, and we're not missing anything. I mean, we're talking about potentially huge data transfers here, and we need to be bulletproof.

1.  **`AccountRecordSet`:** The import of account attributes is handled, and the new `Account::JoinCode` and `Entropy` are created. The checking of the account data in the archive ensures the integrity of the data being imported.

2.  **`UserRecordSet`:** The remapping of user IDs and handling of identities (finding or creating `Identity` records) during import is super important. Using `User.insert_all!` is the right way to optimize this operation.

3.  **`EntropyRecordSet`:** Deleting and re-inserting `Entropy` records is the correct approach to clean up the default one and replace it with the imported values.

4.  **`ActiveStorage::BlobRecordSet`:** We’re carefully handling the `service_name` change between environments. We need to be able to switch between the environments. It's also smart that the `key` remapping is used for the deterministic key, ensuring it’s globally unique and that files are not deleted on rollback.

5.  **`ActiveStorage::VariantRecord`:** *Whoa!* ActiveStorage variants, thumbnails, and everything related is handled by simply exporting and importing the `ActiveStorage::VariantRecord`, the `ActiveStorage::Blob` and the `ActiveStorage::Attachment` records, along with their physical files in the `FileRecordSet`! So, no expensive image processing needed. The record remapping ensures the relationships are correct.

6.  **`ActiveStorage::FileRecordSet`:** Streaming is the right approach for 500+GB archives! Using `blob.download` with a block allows us to stream chunks directly, and the archive checking verifies every file exists. That's solid! We're also streaming uploads without loading the whole file into RAM, which is *critical* for performance and memory. The error handling with the `uploaded_keys` array is perfect to ensure that if something goes wrong, *everything* is cleaned up, including the disk or S3 files.

Okay, I think we are good! This is all very well-thought-out, and the level of detail is impressive. We should be good to go.

Okay, here's the breakdown of my thought process regarding the `Account::ImportsController` and handling large ZIP file uploads (specifically 500+GB!).  We need to support both local and S3 storage, as dictated by `AGENTS.md`, and handle these massive files efficiently.  I'm also keeping in mind the configurations in `config/initializers/active_storage.rb` and `config/initializers/uuid_framework_models.rb`.

My immediate concern is how files get *submitted* to `/account/imports`. There are two main methods: the standard multipart form upload (using `params[:file]` or `params[:import][:file]`), and *direct upload* which uses `direct_upload: true` on the `file_field`. The direct upload method is crucial for very large files since it bypasses buffering on Puma by using Active Storage.

Now, a critical point. I stopped to think about the *untenanted* scenario, `/account/imports/new` when `Current.account` is `nil`.  The inclusion of `Authentication` and `Authorization` into `ActiveStorage::DirectUploadsController` through the `ActiveStorageDirectUploadsControllerExtensions` module could cause a *failure* because it requires a valid account. This would trigger a redirect to `/session/menu` and halt the process. Even if we bypassed the account requirement, the `ActiveStorage::Blob.create_before_direct_upload!` method would try to insert a `nil` `account_id` into the `active_storage_blobs` table, which has a `null: false` constraint on `account_id` and a `belongs_to :account` association. This would also fail with a "Account must exist" error! This is a massive issue.

Therefore, we need to think through two alternative scenarios that bypass these issues.

messages.thinking:
**Deep Dive: Secure and Seamless Account Imports**

Alright, let's break this down. The core goal here is a user-friendly and robust account import feature. We need to allow a user to bring in their data, whether they're a new user or an existing one, and ensure that the process is secure, efficient, and, critically, leaves no trace if it fails.

Firstly, the route. The ability to import into a new account is critical, meaning we need to handle both the untenanted scenario (importing into a brand-new account, which has no ID yet) and the tenanted scenario (importing into an existing, identified account). The potential for route confusion is real, especially with URL segments. The design needs to be robust enough to handle the user manually typing the URL, using a link, or making a programmatic call. Using `disallow_account_scope` and `allow_account_or_unscoped` is the key.

The plan: Allow imports to work regardless of `Current.account` presence. `skip_before_action :require_account` and `allow_unauthorized_access`, then `Current.without_account` for a new account.

Let's also think about the multi-tenant vs. single-tenant cases. We need to support the use case of a user who is *already* signed in on a single-tenant instance and then imports an account, and we also need to support fresh installs. The design must handle these scenarios gracefully, including the default setup script (`bin/setup`) creating a default account. Blocking imports for signed-in users on a single-tenant instance (before the initial signup) is a non-starter.

**The heart of the solution:**

"An import that can't be completed leaves nothing behind" is the guiding principle. Every single detail of the process needs to be thought through.

1.  **Before:** Capture current database counts of all critical models to use in testing (Account, Boards, Cards, Comments, Users, ActiveStorage Blobs/Attachments, and any files on Disk/S3).
2.  **During**: When a user uploads a zip at POST /account/imports, we create a new `Account` associated with the upload.
    *   **Crucially:** the ZIP gets attached to a *temporary* account (or no account) so that if the process fails, there is no association with an active account!
    *   We make use of `active_storage_blobs` and `active_storage_attachments`, along with their `account_id` attributes, making sure that it's bound to the temporary account during the upload.
3.  **Process:** An `Account::ImportJob` processes the zip.
    *   **Success:** On successful import, the uploaded `.zip` is purged, and the user receives an email, with a link to the new account.
    *   **Failure:** The critical part. This is where we ensure the *zero-footprint* promise is maintained.
        *   Files uploaded to disk/S3 are deleted, or should not be created if possible.
        *   The `.zip` is purged from ActiveStorage.
        *   The import's associated *temporary* account is removed (along with *everything* owned by this shell account: files, attachments, etc).
        *   Crucially, every single database change is rolled back because the design wraps the entire process inside `ApplicationRecord.transaction(requires_new: true)`. This includes the creation of new `Identity` records (for example, if someone's import has new user accounts not in the database).
        *   An email is sent explaining the failure.
4.  **After:** The result is exactly the same as before the import started (Account, Users, Boards, Comments, Files, etc. database counts are identical). We must test this rigorously.

**The "ZERO Footprint" Guarantee is Achieved**

The design is based on two key features that make this work.

1.  **All-Or-Nothing Transaction**
    *   The `check` and `import` and all database inserts/file uploads run within `ApplicationRecord.transaction`.
    *   This includes the creation of `Identity` records inside the `UserRecordSet#import` if users are created.
    *   If any part fails, everything rolls back.

2.  **Synchronous File Purge**
    *   Synchronous `purge` of the uploaded .zip ensures instant cleanup.

It is a monotonic sequence generator (like SQL AUTO\_INCREMENT), NOT account data.

Why are blobs and attachments associated with the account id in an import that is meant to not create an account?

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Snapshot bracket for bin/setup's post-prelude phases: run bin/setup in a
# hermetic sandbox where every effectful command is a recorder stub, and
# compare the ordered command sequence and step output against goldens in
# test/fixtures/setup_phases/. The commands goldens are the contract — any
# refactor of how bin/setup dispatches its phases must leave them
# byte-identical, including the exit trailer. Output goldens pin the step
# labels; only the dim command-echo lines may change across a dispatch
# refactor.
#
# The sandbox stubs bin/rails, bin/minio-setup, docker, nc, brew, bundle, gh,
# gum, and ~/Work/basecamp/docker-dev/setup (under a fake HOME). mise is a
# dispatcher: run/tasks/trust exec the REAL mise against the sandbox's own
# TOML (whose task leaves are the recorders), with --skip-tools injected so
# nothing downloads; install/bootstrap/self-update no-op. Requires a real
# mise >= the repo floor on PATH — the same thing bin/setup's prelude
# guarantees on any dev machine.
#
# Invocation (from anywhere):
#
#   test/setup-phases-test            # compare against goldens
#   REGEN=1 test/setup-phases-test    # regenerate goldens
set -uo pipefail

ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)"
FIXTURES="$ROOT/test/fixtures/setup_phases"
REAL_MISE="$(command -v mise)" || { echo "error: setup-phases-test needs mise on PATH" >&2; exit 1; }

WORK="$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/setup-phases.XXXXXX")"
trap 'rm -rf "$WORK"' EXIT
# Physical path: bin/setup canonicalizes app_root with pwd, and recorded
# paths must match it for $APP normalization (macOS /var -> /private/var).
WORK="$(cd "$WORK" && pwd -P)"

pass=0 fail=0
ok()  { pass=$((pass+1)); echo "  ok: $1"; }
bad() { fail=$((fail+1)); echo "  FAIL: $1"; }

build_sandbox() { # build_sandbox <dir>
  local sb="$1" stub
  mkdir -p "$sb/bin" "$sb/saas/bin" "$sb/tmp" "$sb/tmpdir" "$sb/stubbin" \
           "$sb/home/Work/basecamp/docker-dev" "$sb/home/.config" \
           "$sb/home/.local/share" "$sb/home/.local/state" "$sb/home/.cache"
  cp "$ROOT/bin/setup" "$sb/bin/setup"
  cp "$ROOT/saas/bin/setup" "$sb/saas/bin/setup"
  cp "$ROOT/.mise.toml" "$sb/.mise.toml"
  cp "$ROOT/mise.saas.toml" "$sb/mise.saas.toml"
  cp "$ROOT/Brewfile" "$sb/Brewfile"
  : > "$sb/home/global-mise.toml"
  # The sandbox must be a git repo: bin/setup's pre-commit hooks step runs
  # `git config core.hooksPath`, which needs one (and writes only sandbox-local
  # config). The docker-dev fenced-block probes stay unaffected — the sandbox
  # toplevel never equals the docker-dev path, so they skip as before. Init
  # hermetically: host git config (init.templateDir, hooks) must not leak in.
  env HOME="$sb/home" GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM=/dev/null \
    git -C "$sb" init -q

  # Recorders append one normalized line per invocation. STUB_FAIL names a
  # recorded-command prefix that should exit 9 AFTER recording, so the stop
  # point stays visible in commands.txt.
"
}

**Deep Dive Complete: Database, Routes, and File Handling**

Okay, here's the game plan, meticulously crafted to ensure we nail this data export/import feature. First, the database: We're crafting two tables, `exports` and `account_imports`. The `exports` table employs Single Table Inheritance (STI) with two types: `Account::Export` and `User::DataExport`. We'll use the `UUID` as the primary key. We'll set the status enum to `pending`, `processing`, `completed`, and `failed`. We'll add indexes for efficient querying.

The `account_imports` table uses a nullable `account_id` column, which is critical for handling import failures cleanly. We'll track the import status similarly, adding `failure_reason` for debugging, and indexes.

Next, the routes. We'll nest resources under `namespace :account` for account-level exports and imports: This is important. It includes the exact `/account/imports/new` path from the prompt. For user card exports, we'll nest them under `resources :users`. We have to ensure that all generated URLs match what the user is expecting, and that means we must check and double-check, and recheck this, constantly.

Now, let's talk about the core of this: the ZIP files. We'll be using `ZipFile` extensively, with the `ZipKit` gem at its heart. We need to make sure the stream is correctly handled in `ZipFile::Writer`, and importantly, we're adding robust methods for reading ZIP files. We'll ensure S3 support using HTTP Range requests. For efficient memory usage, we'll create custom `ZipFile::EntryIO` to stream even multi-GB attachments without loading the entire thing into memory at once.

We'll design the `Export` model, the base class for both account and user exports. It will use Active Storage, and it will have a "cleanup" method scheduled as a recurring job. We'll define distinct `Account::Export` and `User::DataExport` models, each with specific logic for populating the ZIP file. For user card exports, we'll optimize for batch processing, preloading associations to reduce database queries. We'll stream attachments from storage, deduping filenames to handle cases with two or more attachments of the same name and ensuring the file paths are correctly written. We'll also write card metadata in JSON.

Finally, `ExportMailer` will be used to send out those download links, with the correct URLs based on the export type. It's crucial that the download links work for a day.

Now for a crucial, deep dive. How will the user *actually* download the file? Will the download happen in the browser, or in a test? We have two options:
1.  Redirect from the `show` method: `redirect_to rails_blob_path(@export.file, disposition: :attachment)`
2.  Render a "download link expired" HTML page.

If we *redirect*, a browser click immediately initiates the download, and our integration tests will be clean because `follow_redirect!` will work properly. If the link expires, a subsequent `GET` request will return a `status: :gone` (or 410) since that entry in the database has been removed.

Let's carefully consider this. We must model this and test this. Let's make sure our tests are perfect.

Let's *go*!

{
  "returncode": 0,
  "output": "require "test_helper"

class Users::EmailAddresses::ConfirmationsControllerTest < ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest
  setup do
    @user = users(:david)
    @old_email = @user.identity.email_address
    @new_email = "newemail@example.com"
    @token = @user.send(:generate_email_address_change_token, to: @new_email)
  end

  test "show" do
    get user_email_address_confirmation_path(user_id: @user.id, email_address_token: @token, script_name: @user.account.slug)
    assert_response :success
  end

  test "create" do
    post user_email_address_confirmation_path(user_id: @user.id, email_address_token: @token, script_name: @user.account.slug)

    assert_equal @new_email, @user.reload.identity.email_address
    assert_redirected_to edit_user_url(script_name: @user.account.slug, id: @user)
  end

  test "create with invalid token" do
    post user_email_address_confirmation_path(user_id: @user.id, email_address_token: "invalid", script_name: @user.account.slug)

    assert_equal @user.identity.email_address, @old_email
    assert_response :unprocessable_entity
    assert_match /Link expired/, response.body
  end

  test "create as JSON" do
    post user_email_address_confirmation_path(user_id: @user.id, email_address_token: @token, script_name: @user.account.slug), as: :json

    assert_response :no_content
    assert_equal @new_email, @user.reload.identity.email_address
  end

  test "create as JSON with invalid token" do
    post user_email_address_confirmation_path(user_id: @user.id, email_address_token: "invalid", script_name: @user.account.slug), as: :json

    assert_response :unprocessable_entity
    assert_equal "Token is invalid or has expired", @response.parsed_body["error"]
    assert_equal @old_email, @user.reload.identity.email_address
  end

  test "create as JSON with expired token" do
    expired_token = @user.send(:generate_email_address_change_token, to: @new_email, expires_in: 0.seconds)

    travel_to 1.minute.from_now do
      post user_email_address_confirmation_path(user_id: @user.id, email_address_token: expired_token, script_name: @user.account.slug), as: :json

cat <<'EOF' > app/models/zip_file.rb
class ZipFile
  class InvalidZipError < StandardError; end
  class UnsupportedFeatureError < InvalidZipError; end

  class << self
    def create_for(attachment, filename:)
      raise ArgumentError, "No block given" unless block_given?

      reflection = attachment.record.class.reflect_on_attachment(attachment.name)
      service_name = reflection.options[:service_name] || ActiveStorage::Blob.service.name
      service = ActiveStorage::Blob.services.fetch(service_name)

      if s3_service?(service)
        create_for_s3(attachment, filename: filename, service: service) { |zip| yield zip }
      else
        create_for_disk(attachment, filename: filename) { |zip| yield zip }
      end
    end

    def read_from(attachment)
      raise ArgumentError, "No block given" unless block_given?
      raise InvalidZipError, "No file attached" unless attachment.attached?

      service = attachment.blob.service

      if s3_service?(service)
        read_from_s3(attachment, service: service) { |zip| yield zip }
      else
        read_from_disk(attachment, service: service) { |zip| yield zip }
      end
    end

    private
      def s3_service?(service)
        # The S3 service doesn't get loaded in development unless it's used
        defined?(ActiveStorage::Service::S3Service) && service.is_a?(ActiveStorage::Service::S3Service)
      end

      def create_for_s3(attachment, filename:, service:)
        blob = ActiveStorage::Blob.create_before_direct_upload!(
          filename: filename,
          content_type: "application/zip",
          byte_size: 0,
          checksum: "pending"
        )

        writer = Writer.new

        # Use S3's upload_stream directly for write-based streaming.
        # ActiveStorage's upload method expects a read-based IO, but ZipKit
        # needs a write-based stream. The TransferManager's upload_stream
        # yields a writable IO that we can stream directly to.
        service.send(:upload_stream,
          key: blob.key,
          content_type: "application/zip",
          part_size: 100.megabytes
        ) do |write_stream|
          write_stream.binmode
          writer.stream_to(write_stream)
          yield writer
          writer.close
        end

        blob.update!(byte_size: writer.byte_size, checksum: writer.checksum)
        attachment.attach(blob)
      rescue Aws::S3::MultipartUploadError => e
        if e.errors.any?
          raise e.errors.first
        else
          raise e
        end
      end

      def create_for_disk(attachment, filename:)
        tempfile = Tempfile.new([ "export", ".zip" ])
        tempfile.binmode

        writer = Writer.new(tempfile)
        yield writer
        writer.close

        tempfile.rewind
        attachment.attach(io: tempfile, filename: filename, content_type: "application/zip")
      ensure
        tempfile&.close
        tempfile&.unlink
      end

      def read_from_s3(attachment, service:)
        url = service.send(:object_for, attachment.blob.key).presigned_url(:get, expires_in: 24.hours.to_i)
        ssl_verify_peer = service.client.client.config.ssl_verify_peer != false
        remote_io = RemoteIO.new(url, ssl_verify_peer: ssl_verify_peer)
        yield Reader.new(remote_io)
      end

      def read_from_disk(attachment, service:)
        if service.respond_to?(:path_for)
          File.open(service.path_for(attachment.blob.key), "rb") do |file|
            yield Reader.new(file)
          end
        else
          attachment.open do |file|
            yield Reader.new(file)
          end
        end
      rescue Errno::ENOENT, ActiveStorage::FileNotFoundError => error
        raise InvalidZipError, error.message
      end
  end
end
EOF

class ZipFile::Writer
  attr_reader :byte_size

  def initialize(io = nil)
    @entries = []
    @byte_size = 0
    @output_io = io
    @streamer = nil
    @digest = Digest::MD5.new

  def stream_to(io)
    @output_io = io
  end

  def write(data)
    @output_io.write(data)

    data.bytesize

class Account::DataTransfer::IdMapper
  attr_reader :account, :uploaded_keys
  attr_accessor :old_account_id, :old_external_account_id

  def initialize(account)
    @account = account
    @uploaded_keys = []
  end

  def remap_id(old_id)
    return nil if old_id.blank?
    return account.id if old_id == old_account_id

    old_hex = ActiveRecord::Type::Uuid.base36_to_hex(old_id)
    digest = Digest::SHA256.hexdigest("#{account.id}:#{old_id}")
    rand_b = (digest[0, 16].to_i(16) & ((1 << 62) - 1)) | (0b10 << 62)
    new_hex = old_hex[0, 16] + rand_b.to_s(16).rjust(16, "0")

    ActiveRecord::Type::Uuid.hex_to_base36(new_hex)
  end

  def remap_token(old_token, namespace: "token", length: 28)
    return nil if old_token.blank?

    digest = Digest::SHA256.hexdigest("#{account.id}:#{namespace}:#{old_token}")
    digest.to_i(16).to_s(36).rjust(length, "0")[0, length]
  end

  def old_account_slug
    if old_external_account_id.present?
      "/#{AccountSlug.encode(old_external_account_id)}"
    end
  end
end
EOF

class Account::DataTransfer::RecordSet
  INTERNAL_RECORD_TYPES = %w[Export Account::Import].freeze
  BATCH_SIZE = 500

  attr_reader :account, :model, :attributes

  def initialize(account:, model:, attributes: nil)
    @account = account
    @model = model
    @attributes = (attributes || model.column_names).map(&:to_s)
  end

  def export(to:)
    with_zip(to) do
      export_records
    end
  end

  def check(from:)
    with_zip(from) do
      check_records
    end
  end

  def import(from:, mapper:)
    with_zip(from) do
      import_records(mapper)
    end
  end

  private
    attr_reader :zip

    def with_zip(zip)
      old_zip = @zip
      @zip = zip
      yield
    ensure
      @zip = old_zip
    end

    def export_records
      batch_index = 0

      each_record_batch do |batch|
        payload = batch.map { |record| serialize_record(record) }
        zip.add_file(batch_file_path(batch_index), JSON.generate(payload))
        batch_index += 1
      end
    end

    def each_record_batch
      source = records

      if source.respond_to?(:in_batches)
        source.in_batches(of: BATCH_SIZE) do |relation|
          batch = relation.to_a
          yield batch if batch.any?
        end
      else
        source.each_slice(BATCH_SIZE) do |batch|
          yield batch if batch.any?
        end
      end
    end

    def serialize_record(record)
      record.attributes.slice(*attributes)
    end

    def check_records
      each_exported_batch do |batch, path|
        batch.each do |attrs|
          unless attrs.is_a?(Hash)
            raise Account::DataTransfer::Error, "Invalid #{model.model_name.human.downcase} entry in #{path}."
          end

          check_record(attrs, path)
        end
      end
    end

    def check_record(attrs, path)
      if model.primary_key && attrs[model.primary_key].blank?
        raise Account::DataTransfer::Error, "Missing #{model.primary_key} for #{model.model_name.human.downcase} in #{path}."
      end
    end

    def import_records(mapper)
      each_exported_batch do |batch, _path|
        transformed = batch.filter_map { |attrs| transform_record_for_import(attrs.deep_dup, mapper) }
        insert_imported_batch(transformed, mapper) if transformed.any?
      end
    end

    def transform_record_for_import(attrs, mapper)
      remapped = attrs.slice(*model.column_names)

      uuid_column_names.each do |col_name|
        if col_name == "account_id"
          remapped["account_id"] = account.id
        elsif remapped.key?(col_name) && remapped[col_name].present?
          remapped[col_name] = mapper.remap_id(remapped[col_name])
        end
      end

      remapped
    end

    def insert_imported_batch(batch, _mapper)
      model.insert_all!(batch)
    end

    def each_exported_batch
      zip.glob("data/#{model_dir}/*.json").each do |path|
        parsed = JSON.parse(zip.read(path))
        rows = parsed.is_a?(Array) ? parsed : [ parsed ]
        yield rows, path
      rescue JSON::ParserError
        raise Account::DataTransfer::Error, "The archive contains corrupted JSON data (#{path})."
      end
    end

    def uuid_column_names
      @uuid_column_names ||= model.columns.select { |col| col.type == :uuid }.map(&:name)
    end

    def batch_file_path(index)
      format("data/%s/%06d.json", model_dir, index)
    end

    def records
      model.where(account_id: account.id)
    end

    def model_dir
      model.table_name
    end
end
EOF
